props.title: Krzysztof Kieślowski: I'm So-So

sections.content: This intimate documentary portrait of legendary Polish director Krzysztof Kieślowski, filmed shortly before his untimely death in 1996, offers remarkable insight into one of cinema's most philosophical minds. Coming after his masterful **Three Colors Trilogy** (1993-1994) and during his announced retirement, the film catches Kieślowski in a reflective mood as he discusses his journey from documentary filmmaker to art house auteur. The contrast between his early documentaries like **Personnel** (1975) and his later metaphysical works like The Double Life of Veronique (1991) reveals his evolving perspective on truth in cinema.

sections.content: The documentary's title comes from Kieślowski's characteristic response when asked how he's feeling - "I'm so-so" - which perfectly captures his measured, observant approach to both life and filmmaking. Through intimate conversations and behind-the-scenes footage, we see how his early career documenting life under communism in Poland shaped his later, more abstract explorations of chance and parallel lives. His transition from Camera Buff (1979) to the metaphysical mysteries of **Blind Chance** (1987) wasn't just artistic evolution - it was a philosophical shift in how he viewed reality itself.

Particularly revealing are Kieślowski's comments about abandoning documentary film because he felt it was too invasive of private moments. This ethical concern led him to fiction, where he could explore human intimacy without exploiting real people's pain. This transformation culminated in works like The Double Life of Veronique (1991) and **Three Colors: Red** (1994), where he achieved a unique blend of spiritual and psychological storytelling that influenced filmmakers like Wong Kar-wai and Tom Tykwer. sections.content: The documentary illuminates how Kieślowski's work evolved from social realist documentaries to increasingly complex moral tales. His Dekalog (1989) series marked a crucial turning point, using the Ten Commandments as a framework to explore modern ethical dilemmas. This shift toward examining moral philosophy through cinema reached its apex with **Three Colors: White** (1994), where even comedy became a vehicle for exploring equality and justice. The documentary captures Kieślowski discussing these transitions with remarkable candor, offering invaluable context for understanding his artistic journey.
